claims.claim: On the second day Luther waited at the emperor's court from after four until six o'clock, 'almost smothered for the press'
The evening of the second hearing was 18 April 1521
Köstlin, as cited by Luther's 1930 editors, dates Luther's Worms speech to 18 April 1521
The second hearing was on the day after the first
Luther's own account: 'Then they gave me one day and one night'
The Diet's own record, the Deutsche Reichstagsakten, is cited by Mirbt as his source for the Edict
Foxe names his sources for the Worms account: Melanchthon's history, Sleidan, the Ursperg chronicle's continuation and another (name damaged in the OCR)
Pallavicino says he found matters in the letters of Girolamo Aleander, sent to Germany by the pope on Luther's business
Pallavicino says Aleander reported to Rome on the news of Luther's disappearance
Pallavicino's history is the 1664 revised edition; the first appeared in 1656-1657
The emperor ordered 'a sitting or assembly of the states of all the empire' at Worms for 6 January 1521, and it began that day
The Edict names those present as the empire's 'churfürsten, fürsten und stende jetzo hie versamelt'
Sarpi gives the Edict as saying the herald was sent 'not to know and judge the things that concern Faith, which belongeth to the Pope alone'
Exsurge Domine is dated 15 June 1520
Mirbt summarizes the bull's sentence: penalties for Luther and his followers unless they recanted within 60 days of its publication
Luther burned the bull at Wittenberg on 10 December 1520
Aleander held that a notorious heretic already sentenced by the pope ought not to be heard, and that no safe-conduct was owed
Waterworth: Aleander 'was indeed averse to this summons'
The estates warned that violent measures would 'call forth the greatest commotion' and asked for 'merely ... a summary interrogatory'
The estates' draft grievances say 'achtet man von nöten, das derhalben ain besserung und gemain reformation geschehe'
Buchheim: the estates presented their gravamina to Charles, with the approval of George, duke of Saxony
Frederick asked the legates that Luther's error 'might first be known, before he were made a heretic'
Foxe says Leo sent two legates to Frederick, Aleander one of them
Waterworth: Frederick said the cited works could not, he was persuaded, be from Luther's pen
Luther would recant only if convinced by Scripture and probable reasons
Luther's own account: 'God's Word is not my word, therefore I know not how to give it away'
Charles cited Luther on 6 March 'through the instigation of duke Frederic'
Frederick declined to summon Luther; the citation of 6 March 1521 came in the name of emperor and estates, with a safe-conduct
Luther: 'On Tuesday in the Passion week ... I was cited by the herald'
Luther names the emperor and the electors in person at his hearing
The three spiritual electors were at Worms, by Luther's Table Talk
Albrecht of Mainz signed the ban as head of the Diet
Joachim of Brandenburg spoke to Luther in the talks
Present at the talks: the archbishop of Trier, Joachim of Brandenburg, George of Saxony, the bishops of Augsburg and Brandenburg, Bock of Strasbourg, Peutinger and Dr. Voeus
Frederick of Saxony was at Worms and spoke before the three spiritual electors, by Luther's account
Lewis, elector Palatine, opposed breaking faith with Luther
Philip of Hesse, 'then but a young Prince', said 'is your cause just and upright, then I beseech God to assist you'
Caracciolo and Aleander were at the emperor's residence for the ban, with Mainz and the cardinal of Sion at the signing
Schurff, a Wittenberg lawyer, asked that the titles of the books be read
Schurff asked that the titles be read, by Luther's own account
Caspar Sturm, the emperor's herald, conducted Luther from Wittenberg to Worms
Sturm overtook Luther at Oppenheim to conduct him home
Luther came with perhaps a hundred horse and entered Worms with only eight
Waterworth gives a hundred horsemen and only eight mounted attendants
About twenty-five of Luther's books lay before him
'The books lay on a table which he showed unto me'
Cochlaeus offered to dispute if Luther yielded up his safe-conduct
Glapion ('Sglapian'), the emperor's confessor, had Bucer warn Luther at Oppenheim not to enter Worms
Justus Jonas went with Luther to Worms, by the note of Crespin's editors
Luther arrived at Worms on 16 April
Herrnschmid: 'He came thither, April 16' (the held OCR gives his name as 'John Daniel Hernnfehmid', arminian-magazine_vol-1_1778.txt l.3492)
Foxe: Luther entered Worms 'about seventeen days after Easter'
Eck's two questions: whether the books were Luther's, and 'Whether thou wilt recant and revoke them'
Luther owned the books and asked for time to deliberate
Luther owned the books and asked 'respite of time', by his own account
At the first hearing Charles said 'Costui certamente non mi farebbe mai diventar' Eretico' (OCR: 'Cq^/w cerramaue non mi farebbe mai dinentar' Eretico')
Waterworth: 'This man at least would never make me a heretic'
Luther's plain answer: 'I will not, nor may not revoke any manner of thing ... Hereupon I stand and rest: I have not what else to say. God have mercy upon me!'
Spaniards jeered at Luther on his way to his lodging after the second hearing

On the morning of 19 April Charles declared in a French document in his own hand. He would maintain what his ancestors adopted, 'more especially at the Council of Constance'. He would not hear Luther again

Charles brought before the electors and princes a paper in his own hand, a full sheet long, later read in consistory at Rome. The held OCR ('£ « legger') leaves unclear whether he read it himself or had it read. He would hear Luther no more and would proceed against him 'come notorio eretico'
Foxe gives the emperor's letter 'in effect' on the Friday following: 'we will not violate our faith, which we have promised him'
Pallavicino: 'Tutta la Dieta concorse nella sentenza di Cesare'
Some at the Diet held, after Constance, that faith need not be kept; the elector Palatine opposed them
The archbishop of Trier met Luther on the morrow after St George's day, with other princes
Pallavicino names the archbishop of Trier who undertook to persuade Luther as Richard Greiffenklau (held OCR 'Riccardo Grieffeclau'), a close friend of Frederick but a good Catholic
Dr. Voeus said Luther 'was not called to be conferred with, or to disputation'
The chancellor of Trier dismissed Luther: 'you have leave and licence to depart again with your safe-conduct'
Luther left Worms on 26 April at ten o'clock
Sarpi: Luther departed 'the 26. of April'
Waterworth: 'Luther left Worms on the twenty-sixth of April'
The Edict carries out 'des decrets, Sentenz und verdamnus laut der bullen' and declares Luther 'als von gots kirchen abgesündert gelide und einen verstopten zertrenner und offenbarn ketzer'
After twenty days ending 14 May, no one is to 'hauset, hoffet, etzt, drenket, noch enthaltet' Luther; he is to be taken and sent to the emperor
The Edict orders action against Luther's 'mitverwandten, anhengern, enthaltern, fürschiebern, gönnern und nachvolgern' and their goods
Sarpi's summary of the Edict: Luther's books to be burned, and printing controlled
Waterworth: his writings to be seized and burnt, and works on the faith approved by the Ordinary before publication
Pallavicino: Aleander was charged to draw up the ban, and it was then revised in the emperor's councils
Five of Frederick's nobles in disguise stopped the carriage, took Luther 'con simulata forza', and brought him by night to the Wartburg; Frederick did not know which castle held him
Masked horsemen beat the drivers, made a show of violence and carried Luther to the Wartburg
Frederick 'conveyed Luther a little out of sight secretly'
Herrnschmid: Luther was seized on the road by horsemen and carried to a castle
Steimle: Luther entered the Wartburg on 4 May 1521
Frederick brought Luther to safety 'by means of a stratagem'
The Edict 'found, in general, no responsive reception' in Germany
Waterworth: Charles's departure and the elector's authority 'rendered the Ban ineffectual'
Luther, 1530: the decree was so horrible 'it had to be changed at the diet at Nuremberg'
Luther's Table Talk: the tyrants 'were constrained to recall the same again'
Luther, 1525: the synod at Buxtehude had Leo's bull and the imperial edict issued at Worms posted up against Friar Henry
The Council of Regency, by edict of 20 January 1522, demanded the Edict be carried out
At Speyer in 1526 Ferdinand announced the emperor's resolve to carry out the edict passed at Worms
The Augsburg decree of 1530 announced the emperor's resolve 'to carry out unconditionally the Edict of Worms'
The Edict's date of 8 May matches an alliance of emperor and pope 'to have the same friends and without exception the same enemies'
By the decree 'the emperor procured no small thanks with the pope'
Buchheim: the Peasants' Twelve Articles echo Luther's declaration at Worms
At the Wartburg Luther worked at 'the great work of his life, the translation of the Bible from the original text'
Buchheim calls Luther's refusal 'the official proclamation of the Reformation'
Waterworth tells Worms in his introduction to the Council of Trent
Melanchthon was at Wittenberg during the Wartburg months, so is not on the Who click
Herrnschmid: Luther 'added these German words, Hier stehe ich: ich kan nicht anders: Gott helfe mir! Amen.' (held OCR 'Hier flehe ich'; his name, l.3492, as 'Hernnfehmid')
Carlyle, quoted by Bacon: 'Here I stand - I cannot do otherwise - God be my help, Amen.'
Zinzendorf gives Luther's mind at Worms as 'da stehe ich, ich kan nicht anders, GOtt helffe mir'
Bacon calls the tiles saying 'the famous saying imputed to Luther'
Luther's own account of the tiles: 'although in Worms there were as many devils as there are tiles on the houses, yet, God willing, I will go thither'
Luther, 1522: 'I could have started such a little game at Worms that even the emperor would not have been safe'
Buchheim calls Charles 'a bigoted Roman Catholic at heart' (Buchheim's side)

contested_claims.claim: Whether Luther said 'Here I stand', and in what words
contested_claims.sides: Held tellings that have it: Foxe's English, 'Hereupon I stand and rest' (foxe_acts-and-monuments-v4_cattley-townsend1837.txt l.22078-22079); Herrnschmid, giving the German as words Luther added (arminian-magazine_vol-1_1778.txt l.9300-9311); Carlyle, quoted by Bacon (luther_hymns_bacon-allen.txt l.603-652); Zinzendorf (zinzendorf_sammlung-oeffentlicher-reden-pennsylvania-deu_buedingen1746.txt l.30869-30872). Held tellings without it: Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte1-ita_1664.txt l.10076-10135), Sarpi (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.9625-9680), Waterworth (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.1726-1808) and Buchheim (luther_first-principles-reformation_wace-buchheim1885.txt l.2460-2475). Luther's Table Talk tells no speech of the second hearing; its 'next day' is the talks with 'the Bishops and others' (luther_table-talk_bell1886.txt l.3563-3565). No held editor discusses whether he said it.

contested_claims.claim: Who the Johann Eck who questioned Luther was
contested_claims.sides: The Leipzig opponent, 'John Eckius above mentioned', then the Trier official: Foxe (foxe_acts-and-monuments-v4_cattley-townsend1837.txt l.21752-21753). 'Another' Johann Eck, vicar of the archbishop of Trier: Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte1-ita_1664.txt l.10015-10017). 'The Bishop of Trier's fiscal', without more: Luther's Table Talk (luther_table-talk_bell1886.txt l.3551).

contested_claims.claim: How soon after his arrival the first hearing came
contested_claims.sides: The day after: Pallavicino, 17 April (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte1-ita_1664.txt l.10012-10014); Waterworth, arrived 16 April and appeared on the 17th (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.1720-1729); Herrnschmid, 'April 16. The next day' (arminian-magazine_vol-1_1778.txt l.9150-9151). Sarpi gives 17 April for the hearing but no date for the arrival (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.9617). The fourth day after: Foxe (foxe_acts-and-monuments-v4_cattley-townsend1837.txt l.21734), who gives no calendar date for either hearing.

contested_claims.claim: Twenty or twenty-one days for Luther's journey home
contested_claims.sides: Twenty-one: Foxe (foxe_acts-and-monuments-v4_cattley-townsend1837.txt l.22456-22458, 22484-22485), Sarpi (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.9707-9708), Sleidan as reported by Waterworth (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.1811). Twenty: Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte1-ita_1664.txt l.10357), Waterworth after him (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.1803-1804), and the Edict's twenty days ending 14 May (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.15612-15613, 15620).

contested_claims.claim: The Edict's date and the day it was signed
contested_claims.sides: Dated 8 May, signed by Charles on 26 May: Mirbt, from Wrede (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.15590-15591). Signed in church on Trinity Sunday, 26 May, with the signature dated back to the eighth: Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte1-ita_1664.txt l.10500-10510). Put out on 25 May and post-dated to 8 May: Buchheim (luther_first-principles-reformation_wace-buchheim1885.txt l.2518-2521). Placed under the ban on 8 May: Waterworth (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.1831-1832). '8. of April': Sarpi's English (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.9712-9713), apparently a slip.

contested_claims.claim: Whether the Diet consented to the Edict
contested_claims.sides: Yes: the Edict's own claim of 'einhelligem rat und willen' of electors, princes and estates (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.15598-15600). Pallavicino says the whole Diet agreed with Charles's sentence, and Brandenburg answered for all that the ban pleased them (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte1-ita_1664.txt l.10181, 10494-10500). Also Waterworth, 'with the consent of the Germanic Diet' (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.1831-1833). No: Buchheim, 'without the formal sanction of the Diet', after Frederick and the Palatine had left (luther_first-principles-reformation_wace-buchheim1885.txt l.2509-2521).

contested_claims.claim: The date of Decet Romanum pontificem
contested_claims.sides: 2 January 1521: Mirbt (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.15394). 3 January 1521: Luther's 1930 editors (luther_works-v3-selected_various1930.txt l.288-289) and Waterworth (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.1659-1660).

Aleander drew up its content, and it was then revised in the emperor's councils: Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte1-ita_1664.txt l.10448-10454). Herrnschmid seems to say it was drawn up by Aleander, but the OCR is broken (arminian-magazine_vol-1_1778.txt l.9403-9405). No held source names another drafter, and none confirms Pallavicino independently.

contested_claims.claim: Where Luther stood for his hearing
contested_claims.sides: 'The Senate House': Luther's Table Talk (luther_table-talk_bell1886.txt l.3547). 'The earl palatine's palace': Foxe (foxe_acts-and-monuments-v4_cattley-townsend1837.txt l.21743-21744).

contested_claims.claim: How many grievances the estates brought
contested_claims.sides: 'Four hundred articles': Luther's Table Talk (luther_table-talk_bell1886.txt l.3530-3531). 'Some hundred and four statements': Luther in 1530 (luther_works-v4-selected_various1931.txt l.16043-16045). Mirbt prints only an excerpt (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.15525-15580), so no count can be taken from it.

absent_details.detail: The Diet's own record (Deutsche Reichstagsakten, jüngere Reihe, vol. II, ed. Wrede, 1896)
absent_details.note: Not held; cited only by Mirbt (l.15528, 15590), Luther's 1931 editors (luther_works-v4 l.15992-15995) and others. Searched cic/texts file names for reichstag, wrede, kidd, kostlin, kalkoff, forstemann, balan, brieger, sleidan, weimar, erlang: none. Now a queued want in Build/Ministry/Features/Source-Library/CFT-Wants.md, Era 7, 'Diet of Worms (1521)' (l.368): Wrede's Reichstagsakten or Kidd's Documents.

absent_details.detail: The Edict of Worms in full
absent_details.note: Held only as Mirbt's excerpt of the German text from the Reichstagsakten (mirbt l.15586-15637). The parts on books and printing are known only from Sarpi's and Waterworth's summaries. The full Edict is named in the CFT-Wants Era 7 row for Worms.

absent_details.detail: Charles V's French declaration of 19 April 1521 in its own words
absent_details.note: Not held. Searched cic/texts for 'descendu des', 'tres chrestiens empereurs', 'roys catholiques', 'Kaiser Karl', 'Karls V' and 'Carolus' near Worms. Held only as Buchheim's English extract (first-principles l.2466-2475), Pallavicino's Italian paraphrase (l.10142-10177) and Foxe's 'in effect' (l.22133-22147). Named in the CFT-Wants Era 7 row for Worms.

Not held. Searched all texts for 'aleand' and 'aleandro': hits are Pallavicino, Waterworth, Sarpi, Foxe, Buchheim and Beza's editors, with Brieger's 1884 edition only cited (haupt ZKG 7 l.17946). The Loyola letters' editors annotate him (ignatius-loyola_epistolae-et-instructiones-v22-lat_1903.txt l.9858, 11088-11090). Mirbt cites Kalkoff's edition of the dispatches, not held (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.15592). Two 1538 items name him: a letter in Theiner that calls him legate (theiner_vetera-monumenta-slavorum-meridionalium-v1-lat_1863.txt l.48761), and ZKG 14's notice of Capasso's work on the legates to Vicenza, with six letters, mostly his, printed by Capasso (jacques-de-vitry_briefe-in-zeitschrift-fuer-kirchengeschichte-14-lat-deu_rohricht1894.txt l.24355-24362). Aleander reaches us through Pallavicino, who used his letters. Luther's 1930 editors (luther_works-v3 l.293-294) report one 1520 letter from Aix, not from Worms.

absent_details.detail: Luther's Worms speech in its original Latin or German
absent_details.note: Not held. Searched for 'Wormser Rede', 'Rede in Worms', 'hier stehe', 'kan nicht anders', 'kann nicht anders', 'nec possum nec volo'. The only hits for the text's history are a ZKG 14 news note naming Spalatin's version and Burkhardt's 1894 printing (jacques-de-vitry ZKG 14 file l.25846-25853). The speech is held in Foxe's English.
No list of names is held. The Edict names the estates as a body (mirbt l.15598-15600). Those named in the entry come from narratives, each cited.

absent_details.detail: A held editor's judgment on whether 'Here I stand' is authentic
absent_details.note: None held. Searched LHYM, the Luther works volumes, First Principles, Foxe, Waterworth and the Table Talk for spurious, doubtful, legend, authentic, apocryphal and 'later addition' near 'Worms' or 'stand': none found. The only held caution is Bacon's on the tiles saying (luther_hymns l.856-859). The entry says only which tellings have it.

absent_details.detail: Luther's letters from Worms and the Wartburg
absent_details.note: Not held as letters; only quoted in editors' introductions (luther_works-v3 l.6370-6378). Searched for 'ex eremo', 'Patmos', 'correspondence'; no Enders or Smith correspondence is held.

absent_details.detail: A witness of the time for the opening day of 6 January 1521
absent_details.note: Foxe is the only held narrative that gives it (foxe l.21660-21667); the Herberstein editor gives the day it was called for (herberstein_notes-upon-russia-v1 l.5815-5818). No held act dates the opening.
